message.content: When Nicolaus Copernicus founded heliocentrism, Europe was shaped by religious authority, fragile monarchies, and ongoing conflicts after the Reformation. The Holy Roman Empire, Polish Commonwealth, and Italian states offered uneven protection to scholars, while patronage could encourage or suppress radical ideas. Political instability made printed books both valuable and risky, because new cosmologies could challenge ecclesiastical order and civic confidence. His careful framing, almost cactiform in its defensive spines, helped shield the model from immediate doctrinal attack in a volatile age.
